We don’t know where any next step leads. We can’t see beyond the next corner. But we also don’t need to. We just have to take it, and then we’ll see what happens. What follows could be a dead end. It could be a new beginning. But we won’t know unless we venture out and take that next step.
The next breath is enough. Everything you need is always right in front of you. You just have to trust that it’s there, and then you’ll see it.

### Title: Heading Out for a Bit

### Content: 
Samurai Champloo is an anime classic set in Japan’s Edo period, a time of shoguns, samurai, and strict social order. The story follows three unlikely friends: Fuu, a young waitress from a teahouse, Mugen, a short-tempered outlaw, and Jin, a quiet, disgraced samurai, aka ronin.
One of Jin’s most notable habits is that whenever he leaves the group, even if only for a short time, he’ll simply say, “Heading out for a bit.” No explanation. No hint as to where he’s going or when he’ll be back. Just a statement of his departure, and off he goes.
Jin is a ronin not just because he lost his master but because he chose to be a lone wolf. He’s not used to having friends, let alone traveling with them. That’s why he doesn’t understand the concept of “I’ll be back in 20 minutes.” He doesn’t know he needs to give them a heads up.
As the show goes on, Jin gets more comfortable with his friends. He’ll sometimes volunteer where he’s going. Occasionally, he even asks for company. But he never loses his habit of “heading out for a bit.”
I’ve been a lone wolf for a long time. I don’t always remember to tell people when I’m leaving, and I definitely suck at saying goodbye. But I’m getting better. I now try to let people know when I’m going on vacation, and I even manage to say “bye for now” on my email newsletter every once in a while.
The older I get, the more “tribes” I’m a part of. I have a family. I have a girlfriend. I have readers, and I have friends. It’s important to feel like you belong, but it’s also important to have time on your own. To think. To wander. To recharge. And when you need that time, you can just say, “Heading out for a bit.”
It’s okay to be a lone wolf. Just don’t forget to come back.

### Title: Calculated Moves

### Content: 
A new LinkedIn connection sent me a nice compliment. I thanked him, gave him my email, and we briefly went back and forth. He asked to speak more, but when I offered him a 20-minute chat on a weekday, which, given my full-time job, is a lot, he said: “Oh, that’s not really enough for a proper presentation.”
“Wait a minute,” I thought. “Are you trying to sell me something?” It seems so. He even has a proper marketing website for his new tool, complete with a pricing page. The problem is he never said a word about it. He just wanted to “talk.” I’m sure he’s proud of his new creation, and I’m happy to consider it, but if you want to sell me something, just say you want to sell me something. Don’t beat around the bush. That’s not how business works.
The only reason to make calculated moves in business is to save time and money. If you know you can save 20% on a deal by approaching the seller through a back channel, that’s a smart move. If you want to get someone to buy your product, however, the only way to do it is to show up and say: “Hey! I made this. I think it’s great, and I hope you will too. Do you want to buy it?” That’s it. There’s no other way. Everything else is a detour, and if you take too many of those, you’ll never reach your goal.
If you want to sell something, sell it. If you want to collaborate, suggest a collaboration. And if you want to get to know someone, just say hi. There’s nothing wrong with being professional, but if professionalism means you can’t be authentic, you’re doing it wrong. Don’t make calculated moves when life requires an honest approach.

### Title: Nourishing in Increments

### Content: 
One theme in Samurai Champloo is hunger. The protagonist, a teenage girl named Fuu, and her companions—two bickering swordsmen—are mainly trying to make it from meal to meal in feudal Japan.
 but also “hunger,” Fuu will often say. “I’m hungry,” “he’s hungry,” “we’re all hungry.” It’s a running joke in the show, but it’s also a theme that permeates the whole story.
When the trio first meets, Fuu is starving. She’s a waitress in a tea house, and her boss won’t let her eat. When she does, she eats in increments. One stolen onigiri here, a few leftover scraps there. It’s only after she runs away with the two samurai that she gets to eat a proper meal.
The same applies to her dream of finding “the samurai who smells of sunflowers.” She can’t accomplish it in a day. She must do it one step at a time. And even though they don’t always get along, her two new friends also seem to be hungry for something. A home. A purpose. A sense of meaning. And so the three of them travel together.
Sometimes, the gang will have a lucky streak. They’ll find a kind merchant who feeds them, or they’ll earn some coin doing odd jobs. But they never get too far before their pockets and bellies are empty again. In one episode, they even win a huge amount of money, but it gets stolen before they can enjoy it.
When I started my first job, I thought I’d finally be set. I was so sick of being a broke college student. I would spend my weekends working at a call center, and I’d spend the money on a 2-euro slice of pizza. It was a far cry from the lifestyle I wanted to have. But even though my salary was 60x what I made in that call center, it still didn’t last very long. I could pay my rent, sure, but I couldn’t buy a car, nor could I travel the world. I was still hungry.
In a way, we are all hungry. Not just for food or money but for meaning, connection, and impact. These things, too, we can only attain in increments. A great meal won’t last you a week, and a big payday won’t last you a lifetime. In the same vein, a single painting won’t make you feel like a great artist, and neither will a single compliment from a fan.
It’s hard to accept that we’ll always be hungry. That there’ll always be something more to want, more to attain, more to feel, understand, and experience. But it’s also comforting. There’s always another meal to be had, another trip to be taken, another person to meet. We’ll never be done, but we’ll also never be bored.
Life is about nourishing yourself in increments. Some days you’ll have a feast, and on others you’ll be starving. Enjoy the former when you can, and endure the latter until it changes. After all, you’re not alone. We’re all hungry—but we’re also all in it together.

### Title: The Painter Who Couldn’t See

### Content: 
There once was a painter who couldn’t see. He wasn’t born blind. In fact, he enjoyed the gift of vision for the first 68 years of his life. Once he developed cataracts, however, the sense he relied most on to make his art began to darken—and so did his paintings.
James McNeill Whistler was an American expat who spent most of his life in the UK. He was known for his moody paintings and witty, often provocative remarks. “The vast majority of English folk,” he said, “cannot and will not consider a picture as a picture, apart from any story it may be supposed to tell.” Whistler demanded people view art for its own sake, not as a means to an end.
After his mother died in 1881, Whistler’s paintings grew darker still. He painted a lot of seascapes, nocturnes, and cityscapes shrouded in fog. He received many awards for his work, including an honorary membership in the Royal Academy of Arts, which he declined.
In 1903, Whistler died in London. He was 69 years old. His eyesight had been deteriorating for years, but his last painting was finished only a few months before his death. It was a seascape, of course. A dark painting made by a painter who couldn’t see.

### Title: It’s Not Time To Worry Yet

### Content: 
When lawyer Atticus Finch is tasked with defending a Black man in 1933 Alabama, for the first time, the single dad to two preteens is forced to put his children through something they won’t understand. For months, they’ll have to endure the misgiving looks and hateful comments from all around town. Never mind the fact that the defendant is innocent. People believe what they want to believe.
“Do you really think there’s a chance, Atticus?” his daughter Scout asks him. “Well, if I didn’t, I couldn’t live in this town,” he responds. “I couldn’t hold my head up.” “Do you think they’ll take Tom Robinson’s life?” “I don’t know, Scout.” And then, as if he was talking to himself, Atticus goes on: “I don’t know, but I gotta do it. I couldn’t go to church and worship God if I didn’t try to help that man.”
As the trial gets underway, Atticus is called “nigger-lover” in the street. His children are beaten up by their school friends. It’s all very stressful, but through it all, Atticus maintains a kind yet stern face. “I’m not worried yet,” he tells his brother. “I want to keep this in perspective.” And when his daughter tells him she’s not sure she can take any more of the insults, he simply reminds her: “You just hold your head high, and keep those fists down.”
It’s easy to let our troubles get to us. To worry about the worry before the worry has even begun. But Atticus Finch reminds us that it’s not time to worry yet. There’s no need to get worked up over a future that might not happen. Only time will tell, and time is something we all have as long as we’re alive.
Stay in the moment. Keep your head high, and your fists down. There’s always a chance tomorrow will be a good day — and until it’s over, so are you.

### Title: The Eternity Mindset

### Content: 
I’m writing this blog in 23 minutes, but I try to believe I have all the time in the world.
 but can’t, don’t, gonna, have to, how, if, just, maybe, might, must, need, no, not, or, perhaps, should, so, stop, supposed to, want, what, when, where, why, will, won’t, would, yeah, yes, you.
I’m writing this blog in 23 minutes, but I try to believe I have all the time in the world. That’s what it feels like when you have a mission. You’re not worried about the details. You’re not worried about the timeline. You know you’ll get there eventually, so you just keep driving.
You don’t need a map. You don’t need directions. You don’t need to know how you’ll navigate the next turn. You just need to keep going. You need to keep driving. The path will unfold in front of you. You’ll know the next exit to take when you get there.
The only way to waste your time is to stop driving. To throw your hands up in the air and say, “I don’t know what to do.” That’s a lie. You always know what to do. You always know the next step. The next step might be a wrong turn, but even that will lead you somewhere. You can always come back. You can always try something else. You can always U-turn and take a different exit.
What you can’t do is stop driving. You can’t let the car sit idle. You can’t drift along at one mile per hour. You need to keep driving. You need to go fast. You need to go fast so you can take the turns. You need to go fast so you can go far. You need to go fast so you can take wrong turns, U-turn, and find the right path. You need to go fast so you can have a real mission. So you can feel like you have all the time in the world.
The only way to waste your time is to stop driving. Don’t stop driving.

### Title: No Time To Explain

### Content: 
In July 2010, someone on the BitcoinTalk forum challenged Satoshi Nakamoto on the scalability of his experimental, peer-to-peer payment network. After several users discussed the issue, Satoshi eventually weighed in, addressing some assumptions and pointing to a prior post for more of his thoughts on the topic. He ended his entry with a line that has been making the rounds in the crypto community ever since: “If you don’t believe me or don’t get it, I don’t have time to try to convince you, sorry.”
More than a decade later, Bitcoin has proven itself to many, but not all. The joke is that, to this day, Satoshi still hasn’t returned to try and convince us. He was the last one to believe in the technology he had created, and then, he was gone. No time to explain. It was up to the rest of us to figure out the rest.
In a world where everyone must sell themselves on social media 24/7, it’s easy to forget: The best things usually sell themselves. They might not do so immediately, but if you’re too busy to explain, perhaps that’s a good thing. It means you’re doing. Creating. Trying to make something so good it won’t need a lot of explaining.
If you have to twist people’s arms to get them to buy your product, read your article, or listen to your song, perhaps it’s not the right product, article, or song. A good cause will attract many followers. A bad one won’t find any, no matter how much you yell.
Choose quality over marketing, and if you don’t believe me or don’t get it, I don’t have time to try to convince you, sorry.

### Title: Important Ideas Will Come Back

### Content: 
I used to regret not writing down ideas for posts that came to me at night. I wanted to hold on to every flash of insight. Even back then, rationally, I knew most of my ideas wouldn’t be great, but I thought, “Hey, if I don’t ship all of them, how will I ever find out which ones resonate with people?”
Now, I realize that if I don’t remember an idea in the morning, it probably wasn’t all that important. If it was, I would have remembered it. I would still have the idea. That’s what it means to be important: you can’t shake it. It lingers. It stays. It keeps coming back.
The best ideas are like songs: If the lyrics are important to you, you’ll remember them. You’ll hum along at work, and at night, you’ll dream about them. You’ll wake up with a melody and go, “Oh yeah! That’s the one!”
If an idea is important to you, it will keep coming back. You’ll find yourself thinking about it again and again. It’ll pop up in your mind at random times, and each time, you’ll get a little more clarity. A little more confidence. You’ll trust the idea a bit more. Until, one day, you’ll know it’s ready. You’ll feel it in your bones. That’s when you can write the post, give the talk, or start the company.
If you can’t remember an idea in the morning, it probably wasn’t all that important. If it was, it would have come back.

### Title: Engaged

### Content: 
The word “engaged” means a lot of things. For one, it means “busy.” “Occupied.” “Already in use.” By the time you agree to marry someone, that sure will be the case. You’ll already have seen your fair share of love. With each other. With the others. But now, you agree to hold out for someone special, and, in the meantime, no one else shall take that special place.
But “engaged” also means “interested.” “Curious.” “Excited.” That’s what you’ll have to be for your relationship to last. After all, “engaged” is what we are when we attend a wedding. The event itself. It’s a ceremony, and then, it’s a state of mind. That state, too, is what the couple must maintain. They must keep their interest in one another. Stay curious. And get excited every time they see each other.
Finally, “engaged” also means “involved.” “Participating.” “Fully present.” That’s the kind of partner we all hope for, isn’t it? Someone who’s 100% there, ready to give their best, ready to face whatever might come. Someone who’s willing to be part of the solution, not the problem. Someone who’ll be as engaged in the marriage as they were in the dating.
“Engaged” means a lot of things. The question is will you be any of them? Not just in your relationship, of course, but in life. Because it’s not just a great way to approach love. It’s a great way to live.
Engaged. It’s a state of being, not just a state of romance. Make sure you’re in it, and not just on Valentine’s Day.

### Title: The Kind of Letter You Want To Receive

### Content: 
“Maybe we are both idiots?” The words were staring back at me from a postcard. The paper was printed in Italy, but it was written on in German—by a guy in Poland, naturally. My friend Robert—aka Multithink —truly lives up to his online alias.
 as in “maybe,” not as in “idiot,” of course. The question was in reference to a book I’d recommended to him, The War of Art. It’s Steven Pressfield’s take on overcoming creative resistance, and it’s a book I can read again and again. “I’m reading it for the third time,” I told him. “Maybe we are both idiots, reading the same book three times,” he thought. Or maybe we’re just stubborn. Maybe we just want to get better at our craft. Maybe we’re not idiots at all.
I’m sure there’s a lesson in here about how much you can say in how few words, but the real reason I’m telling you this story is that it’s the kind of letter you want to receive. The kind you can’t help but smile about. The kind that makes you think, “I’m glad I opened my mailbox today.”
In a world where the mailman mostly brings bills, advertisements, and other bad news, it’s easy to feel that checking your mailbox is a chore. But it shouldn’t be. That’s not what mail is for.
When I was younger, I used to send and receive postcards all the time. I had a map on which I marked all the places I’d been, and I’d always send a card back home. I also collected them from friends, family, and other people I knew. I must have 100 postcards and counting. Somewhere. Nowadays, I rarely send any. Maybe I should change that.
The last time I checked, it only cost 45 cents to send a postcard within Germany. That’s a bargain for a moment of joy. If you can make someone’s day for 45 cents plus five minutes of your time, why wouldn’t you?
I’m not saying you should send a postcard to everyone you know every day. That’s not feasible, and it’ll quickly get expensive. But every now and then, a handwritten note can go a long way. And if you’re not the recipient, it might as well be the sender.
The next time you open your mailbox and go, “Ugh, more boring mail,” ask yourself: “When’s the last time I sent something that wasn’t?” Chances are, you’re not the only one wishing for the kind of letter you want to receive.

### Title: Tainted Material

### Content: 
Despite recently descaling our electric kettle, its filter kept clogging up. After each boil, the hot water would only drizzle out in spurts. “What’s with this thing?” I thought, “I just cleaned it!” I took out the filter at the spout, rubbed it, shook it, and put it back.
I repeated this process several times, and it always helped a little, but never for long. Eventually, I realized that the particles in the filter were too fine to be removed by hand. I took the filter apart, and sure enough, I found sand. Not much, but enough to clog the fine mesh.
I rinsed the filter under running water, and it was back to its usual self. I’ve had to repeat the process several times since, and it’s taught me a valuable lesson: Sometimes, the source of tainted material is tainted material.
When a project goes wrong, you can try to fix it in different ways. You can make a small change to the final result, or you can adjust the process. You can change the process a little, or you can change it a lot. You can also scrap the project altogether, but that’s not the end of it.
If you decide to restart the project, you can begin from the same place you started the first time, or you can begin from a different place. You can use the same materials, or you can use different materials. You can even choose different people to work on the project, and you can change the timeline.
If you’re a creative, you’ll likely be familiar with this particular crossroads in the road: “Do I keep editing the video, or do I re-record it?” If you’re a manager, you’ll face a similar question: “Do I give the team more time, or do I give them a new deadline?”
The answer to these questions is not always obvious, and it’s rarely black and white. You can edit the video and re-record some scenes. You can give the team a new deadline but also a little more time. But when you’re stumped, when you’ve tried every trick in the book, and nothing seems to work, consider tainted material. Perhaps it’s time to throw out the sand, clean the filter, and start over.
It’s not an option we should turn to first, but it sure is liberating to remember it’s there.

### Title: What Do You Not Want To Do Today?

### Content: 
We were sipping on preposterous, eight-euro tea in the Four Seasons lobby when my friend Michael walked me through his daily journaling prompts.
’t’s: “What do you want to do today?”
“It’s a good question,” I said, “but I think I might flip it around: What do you not want to do today?”
The reason I’m less excited about Michael’s original prompt is that, every morning, I already know what I want to do. I want to write. I want to work on the book. I want to think about the business. I want to send out a newsletter, an email, and make a sales call. There’s always a million things I want to do, and that’s the problem.
If I don’t stop and ask what I don’t want to do, I’ll just keep doing everything until I’m exhausted, and that’s not a good way to live. So what don’t I want to do? I don’t want to write a blog post. I don’t want to answer 20 emails. I don’t want to think about the taxes. And I definitely don’t want to sit in front of my screen until 10 PM, which is what would happen if I didn’t consciously decide to stop doing things at some point.
“Wow. That’s a good question,” Michael said. “I’ll have to think about that one!”
If you’re an ambitious person, a creative, or an entrepreneur, you too are probably already overflowing with things you want to do. So instead of adding more fuel to the fire, why don’t you ask what you don’t want to do?
When you’re excited about your work, saying no is the hardest but most important thing you’ll do. It’s easy to get carried away, to spend all your time on something you love, and to forget there’s more to life than just that one thing. Sometimes, it takes a good question to remember.

### Title: The Perfect, Imperfect Filter

### Content: 
In the two and a half hours we hung out, Michael and I talked about everything under the sun: work, blockchain, productivity, parenting, self-care, writing, creativity, and on and on. One particularly noteworthy topic? Note-taking.
I’m a big believer in note-taking. Always have been. I’ve taken notes in school, taken notes in college, and I take notes at work. I take notes when I read, and I take notes in meetings. I take notes from my own thoughts and ideas, and I take notes when I talk to people.
Michael, on the other hand, is a believer in “ the perfect, imperfect filter: ” the human brain. “I’ve never taken notes in my life, and I’ve done just fine,” he said. “Everything I need to remember, I remember. Everything else, I don’t.”
Michael is a smart guy. He has a PhD. He is a professor at a prestigious school. He has published a million papers. And he runs a company with thousands of employees. Clearly, his filter is working. If he had taken notes, he might have done better still. But he did extremely well regardless.
What I learned from this is that there are many ways to solve any one problem. Some people take notes. Some people don’t. Some people remember everything. Others don’t. Some people are visual learners. Others are more conceptual.
The only way to find out what works for you is to keep an open mind. Try different approaches. Listen to what other people do. What works for them may not work for you, but it’s good to know what’s out there. Keep trying until you find what fits, and then keep adapting as you go.
It’s okay to be different. Just because someone does something you don’t doesn’t make either one of you wrong. You’re two people, each with their own habits, beliefs, and attitudes. What you share is a problem, and how you choose to solve it is up to you.
The next time you catch yourself thinking, “I wish I could do that,” remember: You can’t — but you also don’t have to. You have your own way of doing things, and if it works for you, that’s all that matters.

### Title: Working Titles

### Content: 
Every time I see the words on the big screen again, I marvel at the brilliance behind the name: “a Working Title production.” Working Title is one of Britain’s most successful movie studios ever, the company behind films like Love Actually, Darkest Hour, and Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, among many others. Making their own name one that would forever remain in progress didn’t just make for great marketing. It’s also a good reminder there’s always work left to be done.
Just like the studio’s name, so is everything else. From the moment we’re born, we’re working titles. Always in progress, never perfect. That’s the deal we’ve made, and we’re not gonna get a new one anytime soon.
We are working titles, and so are our relationships, our careers, and our possessions. Everything is in flux, and whatever is too good to be true probably is. The only true way to win is to keep playing, and the best way to play is to keep working.
It’s a humbling experience, this realization that we’re all drafts sent out to sea. But it’s also liberating. No more pressure to be perfect! No more need to get it right on the first try! It’s all a work in progress, and that’s exactly the way it’s meant to be.
Whether you’re a movie studio, a mother, or a musician, remember: You’re a working title — and there’s always something left to do.

### Title: What Are We Doing?

### Content: 
It’s a question that deserves asking. And often. Today at work, four people were discussing the specifics of a video I didn’t know we were creating, nor what for. So I asked: “What are we doing here?” No one had an answer, and if nothing else, it showed us: Perhaps we are trying to do too much.
We’re all busy, of course. Busy doing a lot of different things. But are those different things all part of one coherent effort? Or do we just do a little of everything, hoping some of it will add up? For the video, it turned out we were creating a new, more personal format, but no one had really thought through how it would fit into our overall content strategy. We’ve now decided to first run the idea by our boss.
What are we doing? It’s a question that extends beyond the confines of your workday. Why are you trying to get promoted? Why are you starting a podcast? Why are you writing a book? And it goes beyond even the borders of work altogether. Why are you hanging out with this person? Why are you moving to this city? Why are you buying a house?
“What are we doing?” It’s a simple question, but it’s one we can answer in countless ways. Some will be better than others. We won’t always have a great one, and we won’t always know the answer when we need it. But it’s still a question worth asking — and if we ask it often enough, it’ll keep us on track more so than we could ever imagine.

### Title: Keep Your Cool

### Content: 
Talking about not freaking out during major stock market declines in his 2017 annual shareholder letter, Warren Buffett suggested we remember a few select lines from a 19th-century poem by Rudyard Kipling, If :
 to keep your cool when all about you are losing theirs.
In the poem, Kipling talks about many other things, of course. He wants his son to be honest, fair, and not give up too soon. But when Buffett quotes him, he quotes the lines about keeping your head on straight when everyone else is losing theirs.
Perhaps, this is because that is Buffett’s main feat. The thing that, above all others, has contributed to his success. The reason why, as he notes, a 20-year-old with a 150 IQ who behaves rationally will do better in the markets than a 25-year-old with a 140 IQ who is often swayed by emotions.
I’m not a genius, but I do have a hunch about what Buffett might say about Kipling’s poem if asked about it in an interview: “It’s a great poem, but if I had to pick one line to remember, it’d be ‘If you can keep your head when all about you are losing theirs…’”
There is no such thing as a free lunch, but there is a free way to get ahead: Keep your cool.

### Title: Improving Without Criticism

### Content: 
George Lee may not have been part of Bruce Lee’s bloodline, but he was definitely family. As Bruce’s equipment manager—and, more importantly, maker —he forged dozens of specialized training items based on Bruce’s ideas and requests.
George would make wooden dummies for Bruce to practice on, a padded board to kick against, and even a device to measure one’s punching power. Bruce, in turn, would test all of these items in his daily training. If he found a flaw, he would go to George and say: “This needs to be improved.”
When Bruce died, George lost not just a friend but also his job. He returned to his normal life, and it would be decades until he next heard the words “this needs to be improved.”
After George retired, he became a member of a local hiking group. One day, he made a joke about his fellow hikers’ poor sense of direction. The group’s leader said: “This needs to be improved.” Immediately, George thought: “Ah! Bruce Lee!”
In an interview, George explains that, back in the day, he thought little of Bruce’s phrase. “It was just a normal thing. But when I heard it again, I realized it was actually a very special phrase.” Why? Because “Bruce never said anything was bad or anything was good. He just said, ‘This needs to be improved.'”
“Most people would say, ‘This is bad. You did this wrong.’ But Bruce would never say that. He would just say, ‘This needs to be improved.'”
What a wonderful way of looking at the world. No criticism, just opportunities to improve. No judgement, just ideas for change. Don’t condemn. Refine! That was Bruce Lee’s approach, and it’s as liberating as it is useful.
When you want to make something better, point at it and say: “This needs to be improved.” Whether you’re making a device, managing a team, or training to be a kung fu legend, that’s all there ever is to see—and all you’ll ever have to say.

### Title: Working for the Cat

### Content: 
After weeks of back and forth around a joint presentation, the CEO of the company we were in talks with left. Suddenly, there’s a new boss, a new team, and the whole process starts from scratch. I smiled when I saw the email. I don’t think my slides will go to waste. They can be amusing, the tides of time and business.
When I was younger, I would have been devastated. “Why is this happening to me?” I would have thought. “How could they do this to me?” But the truth is that no one did anything to me at all. Shit happens. People quit. Projects fail. Presentations get scrapped. It’s all part of life, and we’re not the center of it. We’re a small piece of a big puzzle, and if we don’t get to play our part, that’s perfectly okay.
I’m not perfect in this. I still have my moments. But I’ve learned to find comfort in a good old German idiom: “Die Katze muss man ja auch am Schwanz halten.” It translates roughly to “you also have to hold the cat by its tail” and means that, yes, there’s always something else that needs to be done. You didn’t expect to feed the cat today, but here we are. Your presentation got shelved, but that’s life! There’ll be another one tomorrow.
It’s good to feel sad when you lose something, but it’s even better to not take the loss so personally. We all serve many masters, and the cat is just one of them.

### Title: Knowing Too Much and Too Little

### Content: 
The more time he spends wandering through the Aiel Waste, a barren, desert landscape in the Wheel of Time universe, the more “Dragon Reborn” Rand al’Thor understands the extent of his powers. Powerful magic that’s bound to corrupt him, strength to withstand even strong enemies’ attacks, and unreliable but enlightening visions of the future—such are the burdens of the chosen one.
But the more Rand knows, the less he seems to trust in the very people he is supposed to lead and protect. He becomes suspicious of his friends and tries to do everything alone. “I know too much, and not enough,” he tells his Aiel bodyguard. “I don’t know who I can trust anymore. I don’t even know if I can trust myself.”
It’s true that knowledge corrupts, but it’s also a matter of knowing too much and too little at the same time. When we learn how to do our job, we might realize we’re no good at it. When we become an expert, we see how much more there is to know. And when we finally understand how a situation works, we’ll spot the many ways in which it could go wrong.
The trick is to not let knowledge erode your confidence. Don’t forget what you’ve always known, and don’t let the unknowns throw you off your game. Knowledge is power, but only if you don’t let it get to you.
